# Co-Evolutionary Predator-Prey Simulation with MAPPO Final submission package for a continuous 2D predator-prey ecosystem in which both species learn decentralized policies through multi-agent reinforcement learning. [![Predator-prey simulation demonstration](assets/demo-preview.gif)](https://han-chh.github.io/Pred-Prey-Simulation-System--MARL-based/) **[▶ Watch the full 10-minute presentation video](https://han-chh.github.io/Pred-Prey-Simulation-System--MARL-based/)** — click the animated preview or this link to open the browser player. The original 4K MP4 remains available in the repository through Git LFS. The project combines: - an energy-based agent simulation with food, predation, reproduction, lunging, local vision, and periodic boundaries; - a Python MAPPO training pipeline using centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE); - species-specific actor networks and centralized critics; - a browser-based visual demonstration with live population and energy monitoring; - a deterministic, headless Node.js evaluator for checkpoint and cross-play experiments; - checkpoints, browser-ready weights, TensorBoard logs, raw experiment data, figures, a research paper, and a presentation video. ## Research question The system studies how predator and prey policies co-adapt under individual-level reward optimization, and whether training produces stable coexistence or emergent population-level behaviour. Predators learn a single-stream pursuit policy. Prey use a gated two-stream actor that blends foraging and evasion decisions. Each policy receives a fixed-length, egocentric local observation; the centralized critic receives global state only during training. Actions contain a two-dimensional movement direction and a lunge control value. The environment begins with 30 prey, 10 predators, and renewable food in an `8300 × 6000` toroidal world. Energy affects movement, vision, reproduction, and survival. ## Main findings Ten evaluation episodes were run for each paired checkpoint, with a maximum of 20,000 simulation steps per episode. | Paired policies | Extinction rate | Mean extinction step | Predator lunges / 1K steps | |---|---:|---:|---:| | 0M (Perlin baseline) | 100% | 9,227.9 | 0.00 | | 4M | 100% | 4,733.2 | 97.37 | | 8M | 100% | 7,002.4 | 121.01 | | 12M | 100% | 8,808.2 | 297.51 | | 16M | 100% | 9,851.1 | 21.14 | | 20M | 100% | 7,433.3 | 0.11 | | 24M | 100% | 6,501.1 | 0.00 | Under the submitted environment configuration, every paired run ended in extinction. Transient stability was nevertheless non-monotonic: it fell sharply at 4M, peaked at 16M, and declined again at later checkpoints. The recorded analyses also identify: - predator spatial contraction and grouping at later checkpoints; - prey dispersion under stronger late-stage predation pressure; - improved prey foraging during intermediate training; - a predator lunge strategy that emerged, peaked near 12M, and was later suppressed; - no clear chase/evasion improvement from the original progress metrics, motivating asymmetric cross-play and improved behavioural measures. ![Mean extinction step across paired checkpoints]() The paper gives the full methodology, equations, figures, interpretation, limitations, and references. ## Submission contents ```text . ├── README.md ├── presentation video.mp4 ├── LICENSE ├── assets/ │ └── demo-preview.gif ├── docs/ │ ├── index.html │ ├── poster.jpg │ └── presentation.mp4 # browser-streamable 720p edition ├── Paper/ │ ├── Co-Evolutionary Dynamics and Emergent Behaviors in a │ │ Multi-Agent Reinforce Learning Predator–Prey System.docx │ └── AI Usage Logs.docx ├── all weights/ │ ├── predator_{4M,8M,12M,16M,20M,24M}.json │ └── prey_{4M,8M,12M,16M,20M,24M}.json └── code/ ├── index.html # browser demonstration ├── style.css ├── config/ # world and training configuration ├── js/ # visual simulator and JS inference │ ├── experiment/ # headless evaluation and results │ └── weights/ # default and checkpoint weights ├── py_training/ # Python environment and MAPPO trainer ├── final evaluation/ # checkpoints, logs, and training figures └── docs/ # focused training/conversion notes ``` Important artifacts: - [Research paper]() - [AI usage log]() - [Presentation video]() — 10 minutes 23 seconds, 3320 × 2160 - [All exported checkpoint weights]() - [Python training code]() - [Browser simulation]() - [Raw paired-checkpoint evaluation data]() - [Paired and asymmetric evaluation data]() - [Experiment figure gallery]() - [TensorBoard-derived training figures]() - [PyTorch checkpoints]() The package contains 580 CSV files, 119 generated PNG figures, 12 browser-ready checkpoint-weight files, and six unique PyTorch checkpoints. The `.pt` checkpoints are duplicated under `code/py_training/training/checkpoints/` and `code/final evaluation/data/checkpoints/` for training and submission organization. ## Quick start: browser demonstration No build step is required. Serve the `code/` directory over HTTP because ES modules and JSON weight loading do not work reliably from a `file://` URL. ```bash cd code python3 -m http.server 8000 ``` Open [http://localhost:8000](http://localhost:8000). The simulation starts in exploration mode. In the **Agent Intelligence** panel: 1. Leave **Use model weights at default location** enabled. 2. Turn on the prey and/or predator brain. 3. Use **Pause** and **Reset** to inspect the simulation. 4. Select agents to display their vision ranges. 5. Turn both brains off to enable the manual prey/predator lunge test buttons. You can clear the default-weight option and choose any compatible JSON file from `all weights/` to compare checkpoints. > The default browser files, `code/js/weights/predator_weights.json` and `prey_weights.json`, contain the **12M** policies. To demonstrate the final trained pair, manually select `predator_24M.json` and `prey_24M.json`. ## Python environment The submitted environment targeted Python 3.10.19. Create a Python 3.10 environment, then install: ```bash python -m pip install torch numpy tensorboard matplotlib ``` `code/requirements.txt` records the same dependencies, but its first line (`python==3.10.19`) documents the interpreter version rather than an installable PyPI package. The training configuration is centralized in: - `code/config/worldConfig.json` for ecosystem physics and population rules; - `code/config/trainConfig.json` for MAPPO architecture, rewards, logging, and optimization. Selected training settings: | Setting | Value | |---|---:| | Total environment steps | 24,000,000 | | Parallel environments | 8 | | Episode length | 1,000 | | Observation dimension | 40 | | Action dimension | 3 | | Hidden dimension | 256 | | PPO epochs | 8 | | Batch size | 256 | | Actor / critic learning rate | 0.0005 / 0.0010 | | Discount / GAE λ | 0.99 / 0.95 | | PPO clip | 0.15 | The trainer automatically selects Apple MPS, CUDA, or CPU in that order. ## Train or resume MAPPO Run commands from `code/`: ```bash cd code python -m py_training.training.train ``` Resume from the highest numbered checkpoint in the configured checkpoint directory: ```bash python -m py_training.training.train --auto_resume ``` Resume from a specific checkpoint: ```bash python -m py_training.training.train \ --resume py_training/training/checkpoints/checkpoint_step_16000000.pt ``` Monitor a run: ```bash tensorboard --logdir py_training/training/logs ``` Training checkpoints contain predator and prey actors, centralized critics, optimizer state, learning-rate scheduler state, the global step, and random-number-generator state. ## Export PyTorch actors for browser inference From `code/`, the single-checkpoint converter writes browser-ready JSON files to `js/weights/`: ```bash python py_training/training/utils/convert_weights.py ``` The submitted converter currently selects `checkpoint_step_12000000.pt` as its default source. `convert_weights_batch.py` exports all six stored checkpoints after its input and output path constants are set to the local repository. The exported JSON format contains metadata plus named tensors. The JS inference engine reproduces the predator MLP and the prey gated dual-stream actor using `Float32Array` operations. ## Run a headless evaluation The primary evaluator is portable when all paths are supplied explicitly. From `code/`: ```bash node js/experiment/run_experiment.js \ --config config/trainConfig.json \ --constants js/constants.js \ --weightsPred "js/weights/all weights/predator_24M.json" \ --weightsPrey "js/weights/all weights/prey_24M.json" \ --episodes 1 \ --maxSteps 20000 \ --seed 42 \ --out js/experiment/my_run ``` Each episode produces: ```text episode_N/ ├── summary.json ├── timeseries.json └── timeseries.csv ``` The evaluator records population, energy, births, deaths, captures, food intake, lunge behaviour, nearest-neighbour distance, and chase/evasion/foraging progress. Runs terminate on species extinction or the requested step limit. To reproduce the seven paired-checkpoint groups (0M plus 4M–24M), ten seeds per group: ```bash node js/experiment/run_batch_experiments.js \ --config config/trainConfig.json \ --constants js/constants.js \ --weightsDir "js/weights/all weights" \ --episodes 10 \ --maxSteps 20000 \ --seed 42 \ --out js/experiment/output ``` The 0M condition uses seeded Perlin exploration; trained conditions use deterministic policy inference. ## Evaluation data and figures `code/js/experiment/output/{0M,...,24M}/` contains the 70 principal evaluation runs. Per-run and aggregate files preserve: - extinction outcome and step; - natural population growth in 100-step bins; - prey and predator nearest-neighbour distance; - chase, evasion, and forage progress; - lunge frequency and duration; - full step-level metrics. Additional paired and asymmetric tests are under: - `code/js/experiment/paired/paired_0M/` - `code/js/experiment/paired/paired_24M/` - `code/js/experiment/non-paired/prey0M-pred0M/` - `code/js/experiment/non-paired/prey0M-pred24M/` - `code/js/experiment/non-paired/prey24M-pred0M/` - `code/js/experiment/non-paired/prey24M-pred24M/` Generate the experiment plots from the stored CSV data: ```bash python js/experiment/graph/plot_experiments.py \ --input js/experiment/output \ --outdir "js/experiment/graph/graph pngs" ``` The final-evaluation folder also includes the original TensorBoard event files, a merged log, and 48 exported plots covering rewards, losses, optimization diagnostics, population dynamics, resources, encounters, and behavioural metrics. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR E["Continuous 2D ecosystem"] --> O["Local, egocentric observations"] O --> PA["Predator actor
single-stream MLP"] O --> QA["Prey actor
gated forage/evasion streams"] PA --> A["Direction + lunge action"] QA --> A A --> E E --> S["Global state during training"] S --> C["Centralized species critics"] C --> M["MAPPO / PPO updates"] M --> PA M --> QA PA --> X["JSON export"] QA --> X X --> B["Browser demo"] X --> H["Headless evaluator"] ``` The Python environment and browser simulation implement the same core ecological model. The headless evaluator directly reuses the browser `World` implementation so that visual and non-visual experiments share the same update dynamics. ## Verification and portability notes - The headless evaluator was smoke-tested with the supplied 12M default weights and produced JSON/CSV output successfully. - All Python source files pass syntax compilation. - Several older helper scripts still contain the original absolute path `/Users/hankchen/Desktop/code`. This affects the JS consistency test, batch weight converter, paired/non-paired convenience runners, and some plotting defaults. Supply CLI paths where supported or update those constants before running the helpers from another location. - The main `run_experiment.js` and `run_batch_experiments.js` workflows are portable with the explicit commands shown above. ## Further reading - [Training guide]() - [Model conversion and JS inference guide]() - [Headless evaluator notes]() - [TensorBoard merge and export notes]() ## License This project is available under the [MIT License](LICENSE). ## Author Hank Chen — student ID 22230
